title: Answering the Watchtower
short: the Watchtower’s case against the Trinity

keyTerms.d: In the third clause of John 1:1, the Greek word theos (“God”) lacks the definite article, whereas the second clause — “the Word was with God” — has it. The absence of the article is a real feature of the text, and it is doing real work: the article-less theos does safeguard a distinction — the Word is not the person of the Father.

Anarthrous predicate nouns that precede the verb — exactly the construction in John 1:1c — have a primary force that is usually qualitative: they describe the nature of the subject rather than identifying or counting it. In John 1:1c theos is neither definite nor indefinite but qualitative — the Word possesses the full nature of deity that the Father possesses, while remaining personally distinct from him.

Colwell observed that definite predicate nouns preceding the verb usually lack the article. His rule describes what happens to nouns already known to be definite; it does not run in reverse to prove that an anarthrous pre-verbal noun must be definite. Leaning on it to prove “the Word was the God” is a genuine overreach, and an attentive Witness will catch it.

Greek prōtotokos, like the Hebrew bekhor behind it, carries a second and very common meaning — preeminence, the rank and inheritance rights of the firstborn heir — and which sense is in play is settled by context, not by the bare phrase. The word is a title of status.

To make Christ a creature while keeping “all things were created through him” coherent, the New World Translation inserts the word “other” in Colossians 1:16–20 — “all other things” — so that Christ creates everything except himself. But “other” (Greek alla) is not in the Greek text at those points, as the Watchtower’s own Kingdom Interlinear shows in its word-for-word column.

Archē ordinarily means “origin, source, ruler, first cause.” Most translators and lexicographers take it actively in Revelation 3:14: Christ is the source or origin of creation, its active beginning, not its first item.

The distinction between what is true of the Son ontologically (in his eternal nature) and what is true of him economically — in the role he freely took on in the incarnation. Historic Christianity has never claimed that the incarnate Son was, in his human life, functioning as the Father’s equal in glory and office.

Arianism is the view that the Son is the highest of creatures but a creature nonetheless — “there was when he was not,” the slogan Nicaea condemned in 325. Witnesses do not embrace the label, and there are differences in detail; but the structural claim is the same. Against it the historic church confesses that the Son is homoousios — of the same nature as the Father — coequal, coeternal, and consubstantial: one God in three persons.

derive.q: In John 1:1c theos has no article, while “the Word was with God” has one — so the missing article safeguards…?
derive.ans: a distinction — the Word is not the person of the Father; it does not follow that he is “a god”
derive.why: John has just said the Word was “with” God; he is not about to collapse the two. A Witness who insists that clause three cannot mean “the Word is identical to the Father” is correct, and historic orthodoxy agrees: that error has its own ancient name, modalism. The problem is the inference from “no article” to “therefore indefinite, therefore ‘a god.’” That inference does not hold in Greek.

derive.q: An anarthrous predicate noun before the verb usually describes the nature of its subject, from an author whose framework is Jewish monotheism — so “a god” is…?
derive.ans: the one reading the construction will not bear
derive.why: An indefinite “a god” makes the Word one divine being among a possible plurality — polytheism — from the pen of an author whose entire framework is Jewish monotheism. Even were one to retreat to a purely qualitative paraphrase — “the Word was fully divine in nature” — the created-angel Christology has already lost. One who shares the very nature of God is not a creature.

derive.q: Colossians 1:16 gives the reason for the title “firstborn,” opening with “for”: by him all things were created — so the firstborn stands…?
derive.ans: on the Creator’s side of the line — the heir, not the first product
derive.why: The firstborn is the one through whom, and for whom, all created things exist — and a being for whom all things were made, and who holds all things together, is on the Creator’s side of the line, not among the things created. That is why the firstborn is preeminent: he is the maker and heir of creation, not its first product.

derive.q: An angel refuses John’s worship — “Worship God” — yet the risen Jesus blesses Thomas’s “My Lord and my God!” — so the Son is…?
derive.ans: not a faithful angel — he accepts what every faithful creature refuses
derive.why: Faithful angels do not accept worship. Yet the risen Jesus accepts exactly that from Thomas — a confession Jesus blesses rather than corrects, and which the New World Translation leaves unaltered. If Jesus were a faithful angel, that worship was his to refuse, as his colleague refused it; he received it instead.

derive.q: The same Gospel that records “the Father is greater than I” records “I and the Father are one” and “making himself equal with God” — so “greater” is…?
derive.why: The sender is greater than the sent, the Father in unveiled glory greater than the Son veiled in flesh. The reading is not imposed from outside; the same Gospel forbids the ontological interpretation. To make “greater” mean “of a higher order of being,” the Witness must read it against the immediate context that John supplies.

derive.q: The Lord descends “with the voice of an archangel” — and, in the same verse, “with the sound of the trumpet of God” — so the preposition signals…?
derive.why: That the Lord descends “with the voice of an archangel” no more makes him an archangel than his descending in the same verse “with the sound of the trumpet of God” makes him a trumpet. The identification of Jesus with Michael is an inference, and the inference is weaker than it first appears.

honestState.p1: On the grammar of John 1:1, the field is not evenly divided: the qualitative reading affirming the Word’s full deity is the settled judgment of the standard reference grammars and of specialists like Harner and Wallace; and “a god” survives almost entirely outside the academic mainstream. Jason BeDuhn stands nearly alone among published scholars in defending the NWT’s “a god” — and he reads it as a lesser divine being, so he takes the Watchtower’s side and should be answered, not enlisted. That is not a reason to dismiss Witnesses — but it is an honest statement of the scholarly weather.
honestState.fairness: The genuinely live debate is elsewhere: critics such as Dale Tuggy and, on historical grounds, Bart Ehrman argue that the New Testament’s own Christology is more diverse — and in places more subordinationist — than the later Nicene synthesis allows. They are right that the doctrine’s formulation was refined over centuries, and right that the texts must be read without smuggling Nicaea into every verse; the Trinitarian reply is that the raw materials — the worship of Jesus, his inclusion within the divine identity, his role in creation — are present astonishingly early, well before any creed. But Tuggy and Ehrman do not defend “the Word was a god,” the partitive reading of Colossians 1, or the equation of Jesus with Michael. And our own side can overreach: leaning on Colwell to prove “the Word was the God” is a genuine overreach, and the argument from the NWT’s lower-case “the only-begotten god” at John 1:18 does not by itself decide the meaning of any single verse; its only force is to show that the “a god” rendering is theology-driven rather than rule-driven.
honestState.verdict: These arguments establish something narrower than “the Trinity, proved” — one load-bearing piece of it, that the Son is the uncreated Creator, not the first creature; the personhood of the Holy Spirit is a separate case. But on the specific Watchtower exegeses the answer is firm: the key prooftexts, read in their own contexts and even in the Witnesses’ own translation, point the other way. “A god” founders on the grammar and on John’s monotheism; “firstborn” means heir and is explained by “for by him all things were created”; “the Father is greater” is the language of the incarnation, not of a lesser nature; and the worship the Son receives is precisely what faithful angels refuse. One who shares the very nature of God is not a creature: the Word is Creator, not creature.

order: Jehovah’s Witnesses teach that Jesus is Jehovah’s first creation.
That position fails three independent tests: grammar, logic, and worship.
Therefore the Son is the uncreated Creator, not the first creature.

worship angels refuse, the Son accepts

cards.q: State Premise 1 — the Watchtower’s position, fairly.
cards.a: Only the Father, Jehovah, is God in the full sense. The Son is God’s first and greatest creation — the agent through whom everything else was made; before his earthly life, the archangel Michael. The Holy Spirit is not a person but God’s impersonal “active force.” The question is precise: not “is Jesus important?” but “is Jesus a creature or the Creator?”

cards.q: State Premise 2 — the three tests the position fails.
cards.a: Grammar: the construction’s normal force is qualitative, not indefinite. Logic: all created things came through the Word, so the Word is uncreated (Col 1:16–17 makes the same move). Worship: Jesus receives the worship faithful angels explicitly refuse, and Thomas’s “my Lord and my God” is blessed, not corrected.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That the Son is the uncreated Creator, not the first creature — one load-bearing piece of the Trinity, not the whole doctrine. The full doctrine is built from the whole of Scripture; the personhood of the Holy Spirit is a separate case a complete answer must also address.

cards.q: What does the missing article in John 1:1c genuinely safeguard?
cards.a: A distinction: the Word is not the person of the Father. A Witness who says clause three cannot mean “the Word is identical to the Father” is correct, and orthodoxy agrees — that error is modalism. What fails is the next step, from “no article” to “therefore ‘a god.’”

cards.q: Why can’t the construction of John 1:1c bear “a god”?
cards.a: An anarthrous predicate noun before the verb usually describes the nature of its subject rather than counting it. An indefinite “a god” makes the Word one divine being among a possible plurality — polytheism — from an author whose entire framework is Jewish monotheism.

cards.q: Where does the argument from Colwell’s rule overreach?
cards.a: The rule describes nouns already known to be definite; it does not run in reverse to prove that an anarthrous pre-verbal noun must be definite. Leaning on it to prove “the Word was the God” is a genuine overreach — grant it, and rest the case on the qualitative reading and on John’s monotheism instead.

cards.q: How does Scripture show “firstborn” can mean rank, not sequence?
cards.a: God makes David — the youngest of Jesse’s sons — “the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth” (Ps 89:27); Israel, which did not exist at the dawn of creation, is God’s “firstborn” (Exod 4:22). Which sense is in play is settled by context, and Col 1:16 supplies it: “for by him all things were created.”

cards.q: What is the added-word problem in Colossians 1?
cards.a: The NWT inserts “other” in verses 16–20 — “all other things” — so that Christ creates everything except himself; but the Greek has no alla there, as the Watchtower’s own Kingdom Interlinear shows. The unaltered text places Christ outside the category of created things, and a word had to be added to put him back in.

cards.q: Revelation 3:14 calls Christ “the beginning of God’s creation.” Reply.
cards.a: Archē ordinarily means origin, source, ruler, first cause; Christ is the source of creation, its active beginning, not its first item. The same book calls him “the first and the last” (Rev 22:13) — a title Isaiah reserves for Yahweh alone (Isa 44:6). One does not call a creature the Alpha.

cards.q: What is the honest answer on Proverbs 8:22 (“the LORD created me”)?
cards.a: Resist over-reading in either direction. The Hebrew verb (qanah) is disputed, often “possessed” or “acquired”; and the chapter is a poem personifying an attribute of God, which most modern interpreters, across the theological spectrum, doubt was intended as a literal description of a pre-incarnate person at all. The New Testament nowhere cites Proverbs 8:22 to teach that the Son was created; that move is the reader’s, not the text’s.

An angel refuses John’s worship: “Worship God” (Rev 22:8–9). All God’s angels are told to worship the Son (Heb 1:6); Thomas’s “My Lord and my God!” is blessed, not corrected, and left unaltered in the NWT; every creature worships the Lamb together with the One on the throne (Rev 5:13–14). Faithful creatures refuse it; the Son accepts it.

cards.q: Michael and Jesus — what contrast does Scripture itself draw?
cards.a: Michael “did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment” on the devil but said, “The Lord rebuke you” (Jude 9); Jesus rebukes Satan directly, on his own word. And Hebrews 1 is a sustained argument that the Son is categorically higher than the angels — “to which of the angels did God ever say, ‘You are my Son’?” A chapter written to prove the Son is not an angel is difficult to reconcile with the claim that he is the chief one.

obj.q: John 1:1 in honest translation says “the Word was a god.” The second clause has the article for the Father; the third drops it for the Word. The Greek preserves a distinction your translators flatten.
obj.model: Concede what should be conceded: the missing article is doing real work — the Word is not the person of the Father, and orthodoxy agrees; that error is modalism. But the inference from “no article” to “therefore indefinite, therefore ‘a god’” does not hold in Greek. Anarthrous predicate nouns before the verb usually describe the nature of the subject: the Word possesses the full nature of deity that the Father possesses, while remaining personally distinct from him. An indefinite “a god” makes the Word one divine being among a possible plurality — polytheism — from an author whose entire framework is Jewish monotheism. So “a god” is not one defensible option among several; it is the one reading the construction will not bear. And even were one to retreat to “the Word was fully divine in nature,” the created-angel Christology has already lost: one who shares the very nature of God is not a creature.

obj.q: Colossians 1:15 calls Christ “the firstborn of all creation.” The firstborn of the flock is a sheep; the firstborn of creation is part of creation — the first one.
obj.model: Its plain-sense force should be granted: “firstborn of X” can mean the first member of X. But prōtotokos also carries a second and very common meaning — preeminence, the rank of the firstborn heir; David, the last-born of Jesse’s sons, is made “the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth.” Which sense is in play is settled by context, and Paul answers it in the next breath: “for by him all things were created… all things were created through him and for him.” A being for whom all things were made, and who holds all things together, is on the Creator’s side of the line. That is why the New World Translation has to insert “other” — “all other things” — where the Greek, as its own Kingdom Interlinear shows, has no such word. The partitive reading does not hold: the firstborn is the maker and heir of creation, not its first product.

obj.q: Jesus is Michael the archangel. The Lord descends “with an archangel’s voice” (1 Thessalonians 4:16), and Michael leads the armies of heaven as the returning Christ does (Revelation 12:7).
obj.model: The identification is an inference, and the inference is weaker than it first appears. Descending “with the voice of an archangel” no more makes him an archangel than descending in the same verse “with the sound of the trumpet of God” makes him a trumpet; the preposition signals accompaniment, not identity. Many texts show angelic commanders; leadership in battle does not establish that two figures are one. And Scripture draws a contrast the identification cannot survive: Michael cannot rebuke Satan on his own authority but says “The Lord rebuke you” (Jude 9), while Jesus rebukes Satan directly; and Hebrews 1 is a sustained argument that the Son is categorically higher than the angels, who are told to worship him. A chapter written to prove the Son is not an angel is difficult to reconcile with the claim that he is the chief one.

obj.q: “The Father is greater than I” — from Jesus’ own lips. And it’s a pattern: he prays, learns, obeys, dies, calls the Father “my God,” and does not know the hour. Your own texts hand us a subordinate being.
obj.model: Meet it at full strength: it is a pattern, not one verse. But it turns on a distinction the objection collapses — between what is true of the Son in his eternal nature and what he freely took on in the incarnation. He “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7) and was made “lower than the angels” for a time (Hebrews 2:9). “Greater” is position, not kind: the sender is greater than the sent, the Father in unveiled glory greater than the Son veiled in flesh. The same Gospel forbids the ontological reading: Jesus is “making himself equal with God” (John 5:18) and does not retract it, says “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and prays to be restored to “the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5). Not knowing the hour belongs to the genuine limits of his human consciousness, not to a deficiency in the divine nature he never ceased to possess — not ad hoc, but the very logic of an incarnation. To make “greater” mean “a higher order of being,” the Witness must read it against the context John supplies. “The Father is greater” is the language of the incarnation, not of a lesser nature.

unseen.q: The same prayer’s closing verse calls even the Son’s glory “given”: “my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world” (John 17:24). If the Father gave it to him before creation, the Son received his glory from outside, like any creature.
unseen.model: Three things answer it. First, on the sentence’s own grammar “before the foundation of the world” sits inside the clause “because you loved me” — it dates the Father’s love, not the gift of glory; so on the more natural reading the verse does not locate the giving of glory before creation. Second, notice what the disciples do with the glory named in verse 24: they are brought to see it, not to receive it — a different verb from verse 22, where what they were given was the glory of unity — so nothing in this verse extends the glory of being God to creatures. Third, that the Father gives the Son glory is, on this Gospel’s own terms, no concession at all, once we see whose glory it is. The God of Isaiah gives his glory “to no other” (Isaiah 42:8); so a Son to whom the Father gives that glory is, by that very fact, “not another” — not a creature endowed from outside, but the one who stands with the Father on God’s side of the line. A creature is handed a glory that was never its own; the Son is named the holder of the glory that is God’s alone.
